title: Former Meta Manager Sues Company, Claims He Was Fired for Refusing to Sign Immigration Letter
excerpt: James Tillinghast alleges Meta terminated him after he declined to endorse an EB-2 National Interest Waiver petition that he says contained materially inaccurate claims about an employee's contributions.
body:
• James Tillinghast, a former Meta manager, has filed a lawsuit in New Jersey alleging he was fired after refusing to sign an immigration support letter he believed contained materially inaccurate claims.
  • The letter, drafted for an EB-2 National Interest Waiver petition, reportedly attributed $683 million in incremental advertising revenue to an employee whose actual role was in product design and user experience.
  • Tillinghast is seeking over $1 million in damages, including $565,000 in lost pay and $490,000 in lost equity, plus punitive damages.
  • Meta has not issued a public statement on the lawsuit, which was filed in August 2026.

What the Lawsuit Alleges

Around April-May 2024, Meta and an immigration law firm coordinated an I-140 EB-2 National Interest Waiver petition for an employee named Shenxun Wang, who worked within Tillinghast's unit, according to court filings reported by Law.com. A support letter was prepared that required Tillinghast's signature as Wang's manager.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=4wJq89kQFVE

The letter attributed $683 million in incremental advertising revenue to Wang, implied that Wang had created algorithms or AI tools, and stated that Wang managed or led a team or cross-functional group, according to 7Globe, citing the complaint. Tillinghast said he had no data to confirm any of these claims. He understood Wang's actual role to be in product design and user experience — not algorithmic development or revenue generation at that scale.

"Meta later advanced an oral underperformance explanation that Plaintiff contends was pretextual."

— From the complaint filed by James Tillinghast

Tillinghast worked with Wang to revise the letter, removing statements he could not truthfully endorse and keeping only claims he could verify. He declined to sign the broader assertions about national importance, according to the lawsuit.

Termination and Claims of Retaliation

A few months after his refusal, Meta terminated Tillinghast. The termination documents "did not identify underperformance as the reason for termination," the complaint states. Meta later offered an oral explanation citing underperformance — a justification Tillinghast contends was pretextual, according to the court filing.

The lawsuit also alleges that Meta used immigration support as an employment-related benefit and that its allocation was not governed by neutral, consistently applied criteria unrelated to national origin, ancestry, race, or ethnic identity, Law.com reported.

Tillinghast is seeking $565,000 in lost pay, $490,000 in lost equity compensation, punitive damages, and a jury trial in New Jersey.

The EB-2 National Interest Waiver Process

The EB-2 National Interest Waiver is a green card pathway that allows certain professionals to apply without employer sponsorship. Instead of relying on a specific job offer, applicants must demonstrate that their future work in the United States serves the national interest. The pathway is commonly used by researchers, engineers, and tech professionals whose contributions extend beyond a single employer.

Unlike the H-1B visa, which is employer-tied and subject to annual lottery caps, the NIW route places the burden on the applicant to establish exceptional ability and national-level impact. Support letters from managers describing the applicant's contributions are a standard component of NIW petitions.

Broader Context

The lawsuit lands as the Trump administration has intensified scrutiny of corporate visa practices. In August 2026, Anthony D'Esposito, the Labor Department's Inspector General, cited a common practice inside major corporations: managers using the visa system as a private patronage network, The Manhattan Press reported.

The case is separate from other ongoing litigation involving Meta's immigration-related practices, including a Ninth Circuit review of citizenship bias claims in Meta's H-1B hiring and a recent lawsuit alleging the company used AI tools in discriminatory layoff decisions.

What to Watch

Meta has not responded publicly to Tillinghast's allegations. The case could set a precedent for how courts treat retaliation claims tied to immigration sponsorship processes — a grey area where managerial discretion, corporate legal strategy, and individual employees' willingness to vouch for colleagues intersect. For the thousands of tech workers whose green card applications depend on employer-drafted support letters, the outcome will be closely watched.
nri_angle: The lawsuit spotlights the EB-2 National Interest Waiver process used by thousands of Indian tech workers in the U.S. and raises questions about how major employers handle immigration sponsorship claims.
